notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024, as the city reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included. Residents also pay Bernalillo County.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
Debt service leaves out $138,177,000 of principal repaid with new borrowing the city did not spend on capital that year, most likely refinancing or a rolled-over note.
Payments to other governments ($52,141,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.
Political money is not scored: contributions to New Mexico city candidates were not loaded.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 318 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Albuquerque's borders in OpenStreetMap (90 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for New Mexico yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Flock camera network
redFlags.detail: 90 Flock Safety license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Albuquerque's borders in OpenStreetMap. Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is recorded for some; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.

source.label: OpenStreetMap license-plate cameras (as mapped by DeFlock)

redFlags.label: Face recognition
redFlags.detail: The Albuquerque Police Department began a three-year trial of Clearview AI face recognition technology in 2022.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS013576, citing KOB

redFlags.label: License-plate readers
redFlags.detail: The Albuquerque Police Department uses automatic license plate readers. The agency has an inventory of 70 to 80 ALPRs as of December 2023.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS015358, citing Albuquerque Police Department SOP

redFlags.label: Gunshot detection (ShotSpotter)
redFlags.detail: The Albuquerque Police Department employs ShopSpotter gunshot detection technology.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS007503, citing The Intercept

redFlags.label: Cell-site simulator
redFlags.detail: The Albuquerque Police Department accepted a bid of $755,500.00 for "One (1) complete, high-power, multi-protocol international mobile subscriber identity (imsi) and international mobile equipment identity (IMEI) cellular handset identification and location system, collectively identified as a cell- site simulator (CSS) system." The agency has used cell-site simulators since 2012.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS007001, citing ACLU New Mexico

redFlags.label: Face recognition
redFlags.detail: The Albuquerque Police department has been using face recognition technology since 2013.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS004244, citing KOAT

redFlags.label: Real-time crime center
redFlags.detail: The Albuquerque Police Department opened its real-time crime center in March 2011. This RTCC cost $800,000 and was paid through bonds and federal grants. The RTCC has 16 television screens, including a 90-inch monitor, and eight work stations. The center is staffed by four civilian crime analysts, two civilian video production workers, a video intelligence sergeant, a live operations sergeant, and a detective. As part of APD’s overall predictive policing strategy, the RTCC uses a combination of public and private cameras, a face recognition databases, and social media monitoring software.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS006547, citing Police Magazine

redFlags.label: Police drones
redFlags.detail: The Albuquerque Police Department, in 2025, became the first police department in New Mexico to launch a Drone as First Responder (DFR) program.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS018096, citing Skydio
